Enhancement of acidogenic fermentation for volatile fatty acid
production from food waste: Effect of redox potential and inoculum
Jun Yin a,b,⇑, Xiaoqin Yu a,b, Yeer Zhang a, Dongsheng Shen a,b, Meizhen Wang a,b, Yuyang Long a,b,
Ting Chen a,b
a School of Environmental Science and Engineering, Zhejiang Gongshang University, Hangzhou 310012, PR China
b Zhejiang Provincial Key Laboratory of Solid Waste Treatment and Recycling, Hangzhou 310012, PR China
h i g h l i g h t s
 Anaerobic and aerobic sludge were inoculated to food waste fermentation for VFA production under limited aeration condition.
 The maximal VFA yield was achieved at ORP in the range of 100 to 200 mV with anaerobic sludge as an inoculum.
 High protein degradation and VFA yield under limited aeration conditions were achieved.
 The low VFA production from food waste at pH 6.0 under anaerobic conditions was not caused by methanogenesis.

a b s t r a c t
The aim of this study was to explore the effects of redox potential (ORP) and inoculum on volatile fatty
acids (VFAs) production from food waste by acidogenic fermentation. Four experimental conditions with
two ORP levels were tested: limited aeration conditions with ORP level of 100 to 200 mV inoculating
anaerobic sludge (LA + AnS) or aerobic sludge (LA + AeS), and anaerobic conditions with ORP level of
200 to 300 mV inoculating anaerobic sludge with 2-bromoethanosulfophate (AN + BES) and without
BES (AN). The maximal VFA yield (0.79 g COD/g VS) was attained in LA + AnS reactor due to enhanced
hydrolysis of substrates, especially proteins (degradation efﬁciency 78.3%). A higher frequency of phylum
Firmicutes under limited aeration conditions (42.2–48.2%) was observed than that under anaerobic con-
ditions (21.1%). The microbial community was more diverse in LA + AnS reactors than LA + AeS. We con-
clude that appropriate ORP level (from 100 to 200 mV) and inoculum play essential roles in VFA
production.

1. Introduction
At the ﬁrst stage of a typical two-stage bioconversion process,
hydrolysis and acidogenesis of organic matters in wastewater pro-
duce volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and other intermediates by mixed
cultures (Li and Yu, 2011). VFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate
and valerate) have attracted a great deal of interests due to their
wide potential applications, such as in biological nitrogen removal,
bioplastics synthesis, and bioenergy production (Chen et al., 2013).
Therefore, efﬁcient conversions of organic matters into VFAs on
acidogenic stage will improve bioenergy production. Generally,
food waste (FW) with higher biodegradability is regarded as a
desirable substrate for acidogenic fermentation.
Although VFAs offer promise in multiple industrial applications,
the generation of VFAs by fermentation must overcome the
limiting-rate step of hydrolysis and additionally the emergence
of methanogenesis during anaerobic fermentation. By increasing
the hydrolysis and acidiﬁcation rates and meanwhile blocking
the methane generation pathway, VFA production could be
improved (Yuan et al., 2006). Strategies that have been used to
enhance solubilization of organic matters into VFAs include phys-
ical/chemical pretreatments (Uellendahl and Kiaerahring, 2006),
pH control (Yu and Fang, 2003), temperature control (Komemoto
et al., 2009), and addition of enzymes (Cirne et al., 2008). In addi-
tion, the chemical 2-bromoethanosulfophate (BES) is often added
to inhibit methanogenesis (Grootscholten et al., 2013).
In view of current global concerns over acidogenesis, most of
the studies are operated under anaerobic conditions (Komemoto
et al., 2009; Uellendahl and Kiaerahring, 2006; Yu and Fang,
2003). In fact, acid-forming bacteria (facultative or obligate anaer-

obes) carry out hydrolysis, acidogenesis and acetogenesis, which
have different nutritional needs and environmental conditions.
Recently, several studies have shown that limited aeration in
sludge and other organic substrates enhances methane production,
by improving the hydrolytic-acidogenic phase (Xu et al., 2014b;
Lim and Wang, 2013; Díaz et al., 2011). According to the present
studies, low oxygen leads to a high yield and proportions of facul-
tative acidogens (phylum Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, etc.), and high
amounts of extracellular enzymes (Botheju and Bakker, 2011; Lim
et al., 2014). However, due to different approaches to limited aer-
ation for various organic wastes, the optimal limited aeration
intensity remains unknown. Moreover, there is still a lack of stud-
ies concerning about acidogenesis under limited aeration condi-
tions. In fact, oxygen content represents the redox information of
fermentation system, and can be accurately indicated by the redox
potential (ORP). ORP is an indicator of the net outcome of intracel-
lular metabolism dominated by electron transfer and redox bal-
ance (Liu et al., 2013). According to Duangmanee (2009), the
optimal ORP level for methanogenesis is below 230 mV. ORP val-
ues vary between 200 and 300 mV under fully anaerobic condi-
tions (Henze, 2008). But based on Xu et al. (2014a) ﬁnding, the
optimal ORP range for acidogenic fermentation of food waste in
leach bed reactor is between 100 mV and 250 mV, which is
achieved by aeration. However, the detailed information about
the role of ORP in hydrolytic-acidogenic process has not been
shown. Besides, the mechanism about how ORP level inﬂuences
VFA production from FW has not been studied. In this study, we
used ORP to characterize the oxygen-limited and fully anaerobic
environments, with the idea that this would reveal how ORP level
affected the acidogenic fermentation of FW.
In addition, the type of inoculum is a signiﬁcant factor affecting
the evolution of fermentative pathways (De Gioannis et al., 2013).
In a previous study, we ﬁnd higher VFA production can be obtained
by inoculating anaerobic granular sludge than aerobic sludge for
FW fermentation (Wang et al., 2014). However, the work do not
reveal whether differences in inoculum under limited aeration
conditions account for the higher VFA production.
Consequently, in order to investigate the role of ORP level in FW
acidogenic reactors, two ORP levels of 100 to 200 mV (oxygen-
limited) and 200 to 300 mV (anaerobic) were set to reveal how
ORP level affect the hydrolytic-acidogenic phase of FW fermenta-
tion. Two inocula were used to estimate the impact of microbial
composition on acidogenesis under limited aeration conditions. To
determine the effect of BES on VFA accumulation, we also tested
the VFA production with or without addition of BES under anaerobic
conditions. We hypothesized that ORP level of 100 to 200 mV
would beneﬁt VFA production by altering the microbial community.
Here we showed the microbial community analysis, which could be
used to understand the relationship between ORP level, inoculum,
hydrolysis, and acidogenesis in acidogenesis from FW.
2. Methods
2.1. Substrate and inocula
Simulated food waste, containing rice (36%), noodle (26%), cab-
bage (22%), tofu (14%), and pork (2%) was compounded based on
the characteristics of FW in our previous study (Yin et al., 2014).
The ﬁve components came from the same vendor at Cui yuan farm-
ers’ market (Hangzhou, China) and were crushed using a mangler.
The simulated food waste was then stored frozen at 18 C. Before
use, the FW was treated by hydrothermal (HT) pretreatment, as
described by the previous study (Yin et al., 2014). Two inocula
were used: aerobic activated sludge from the secondary settling
tank of the Qige Wastewater Treatment Plant and anaerobic gran-
ular sludge from an up-ﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reac-
tor of the Xihu Brewery (Hangzhou, China). Both of the two inocula
would have to be reactivated with culture medium before inoculat-
ing.

2.2. Experimental set-up
The material in this study consisted of a mixture of 28 g pre-
treated simulated food waste and 7 g inoculum (dry weight) was
in amber wide-mouth bottles (F/M  5.0 g VS/g VS). The working
volume of a reactor was 500 mL and tap water was added to attain
total solids (TS) of 70 g/L. Four operating conditions existed in this
study (Table 2). The reactors were operated under limited aeration
conditions by inoculating anaerobic sludge (LA + AnS) or aerobic
sludge (LA + AeS), and under anaerobic conditions by inoculating
anaerobic sludge with 2-bromoethanosulfophate (AN + BES) and
without BES (AN). By means of limited aeration, ORP could be
maintained in the range of 100 to 200 mV (Xu et al., 2014a;
Lim et al., 2014). So air was added to the reactor at rate of 274 L
air/kg TS/d (according to our previous preliminary test), where
ORP were measured per 2 h to maintain its level between 100
and 200 mV. Nitrogen gas was ﬂushed through the reactors to
create anaerobic conditions, keeping ORP level in the ranged of
200 to 300 mV. BES, when added, was 10 mM ﬁnal concentra-
tion in the reactor. During the fermentation, all of the reactors stir-
red mechanically at 120 rpm using a magnetic stirrer. The
experimental temperature was controlled at 30 ± 2 C and the pH
at 6.0 by adding 4.5 M HCl or NaOH (based on our previous study
(Wang et al., 2014)). Each experiment was performed in duplicate
reactors for 21 days.
2.3. Analysis methods
2.3.1. Chemical analysis
Soluble chemical oxygen (SCOD), soluble sugar, soluble protein,
ammonia nitrogen (NH4
+-N), and VFAs contents were all deter-
mined every 2 days. Total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), volatile
suspended solids (VSS), total nitrogen (TN), total protein (T-
protein), total sugar (T-sugar), lipids (T-lipids) and total chemical
oxygen (TCOD) were measured before and after fermentation.
The fermented broth was separated from the residue by centrifug-
ing at 11,000g for 5 min and ﬁltered using the microﬁltration
membrane (0.45 lm).
ORP values were recorded using an ORP meter (Leici Corp.,
Shanghai, China). TS, VS, VSS, TN, NH4
+-N, TCOD and SCOD were
all analyzed using standard methods (APHA, 1998). T-protein
was estimated from the TN concentration (T-protein = TN * 6.25)
(Yuan et al., 2006). Lipids were extracted by Soxhlet extraction

were determined using a GC7890-II gas chromatograph (Tianmei
Co., Shanghai, China) equipped with a 3 m  2 mm stainless steel
packed column ﬁlled with GDX-103 as the stationary phase and
a ﬂame ionization detector. The temperatures of the column, injec-
tor, and detector were 180, 230, and 250 C, respectively.
Protein, sugar and VFAs concentrations were expressed as the
COD equivalent, calculated based on the complete oxidation of
the individual matter to CO2 and H2O. The COD conversion factors
of protein, sugar, acetate, propionate, butyrate and valerate were
1.50, 1.06, 1.07, 1.51, 1.82 and 2.04, respectively.
2.3.2. Enzyme activity measurement
The activities of key hydrolytic enzymes (protease and a-
glucosidase) were determined according to the method developed
by Goel et al. (1998). The speciﬁc enzyme activity was deﬁned as
unit of enzyme activity per gram of VS.
2.3.3. Bacterial community analysis
Microbial samples were acquired from all reactors at the outset
and end of the reaction, as well as the timepoint with maximum
VFA production, for bacterial community analysis. The genomic
DNA was extracted using an kit (DR4011; Bioteke Corporation, Bei-
jing, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The qual-
ity (A260/A280) and quantity (A260) of the extracted genomic DNA
were determined with a Nanodrop 2000c spectrophotometer
(Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc, Waltham, MA). The extracted DNA was
ampliﬁed using PCR reactions and the universal 16S rRNA primers
F (CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGT
GCTCTTCCGATCT (barcode) ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG) and R (A

community
was

by
Illumina
high-throughput
sequencing. Sequences were aligned and grouped into operational
taxonomic units (OTUs) with 97% similarity. Sequences were then
phylogenetically assigned to taxonomic classiﬁcations and were
allocated into phylum, class and genus levels. Hierarchical cluster
analysis of all samples was performed using R version 3.1.3.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. VFA production from food waste
3.1.1. Effect of redox potential (ORP) levels
Two operating conditions (LA + AnS and AN) with different ORP
levels for VFA production were tested (Table 2). During acidogenic
fermentation, ORP levels were monitored (Fig. 1). As shown in
Fig. 1, under LA + AnS conditions ORP levels were stabilized
between 100 mV and 200 mV after limited oxygen was added.
The ORP levels under AN conditions kept between 200 and
300 mV. To investigate whether ORP levels affect the VFA pro-
duction by fermentation, VFA concentrations in LA + AnS and AN
reactors were measured. As shown in Fig. 2a, on day 3, nearly
two times higher yield of VFAs was observed in LA + AnS reactors
than that in AN. And then VFA accumulation increased rapidly to
about 20 g/L on day 9, which was still two times of that in AN reac-
tors. The maximal VFA concentration was 29.4 g/L obtained on day
17. However, VFA accumulation increased at a slow rate in AN
reactors before day 7. And then the highest VFA production
(18.36 g/L) was achieved on day 17, indicating the negative effect
of anaerobic conditions (ORP ranged from 200 to 300 mV) on
acidogenesis. Jagadabhi et al. (2010) and Xu et al. (2014a) also ﬁnd
the positive effect of limited aeration on VFA production. Low oxy-
gen leads to a high yield and proportions of facultative acidogens
(phylum
Firmicutes,
Proteobacteria,
etc.)
and
improves
the
hydrolytic-acidogenic phase (Botheju and Bakker, 2011; Xu et al.,
2014b). Compared with other previous studies (Table 3), VFA yield
obtained under LA + AnS conditions (ORP ranged from 100 to
200 mV) was 1.3 times higher than that in Xu’s study.
Among the VFAs produced in LA + AnS and AN reactors, 80% of
VFAs consisted of H-Ac and n-Bu, where n-Bu accounted for up
to 60% (Fig. 2b). We attributed this pattern to the >40% total carbo-
hydrate contents of FW in this study, which was consistent with
our previous reports (Wang et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2014). In addi-
tion, another two VFAs (iso-Bu, H-Va) were apparently found in
LA + AnS reactors but were less than 1 g/L in AN. This result
showed ORP levels also would affect the VFA composition, and
there were more kinds of acidogens under LA + AnS conditions.
3.1.2. Effect of inoculum
Combining the results of the ORP levels with VFA production,
we found that an ORP between 100 and 200 mV for the whole
process enhanced VFA yield from FW by acidogenic fermentation.
To investigate whether inoculum affected the VFA production,
anaerobic sludge and aerobic sludge as inocula were compared
under limited aeration conditions. VFA concentrations in LA
+ AnS and LA + AeS reactors were measured. Under LA + AeS condi-
tions, ORP values were above 100 mV before day 6 (Fig. 1), which
could be caused by residual oxygen and the decay of aerobic
microorganisms in the aerobic sludge. As shown in Fig. 2a, in LA
+ AeS reactors, VFA accumulation did not increase before day 7,

which was attributed to less acidogens in aerobic sludge and
higher ORP. After day 7, the VFA production in LA + AeS reactors
increased fast, and ORP declined around 100 to 200 mV due
to the accumulation of facultative anaerobes. On day 11, VFA con-
centration achieved the maximum 17.98 g/L, but was still less than
that in LA + AnS (29.4 g/L). Therefore, under limited aeration condi-
tions, AnS as an inoculum obviously showed superiority over AeS
in acidogenesis. Compared to LA + AnS condition, among VFAs,
iso-Bu and H-Va also accounted for little in LA + AeS reactors
(Fig. 2b). This phenomenon was mostly related to the different
microbial composition caused by the inocula.
3.1.3. Effect of BES addition
BES was added to determine whether VFA production could be
enhanced by inhibiting the methanogenesis under anaerobic
conditions, so two operating conditions (AN + BES and AN) for
VFA production were compared. As shown in Fig. 1, the ORP levels
under AN conditions kept between 200 and 300 mV. However,
when BES was added, the ORP values were generally higher
(between 100 and 200 mV) before day 6, and then dropped to
below 200 mV. The higher ORP levels in the ﬁrst 6 days could
be attributed to that BES (as an extra electron acceptor) addition
would increase the level of oxidation of reactor (Chiu and Lee,
2001). After day 6, some of BES were consumed to weaken this
effect, making ORP dropped. Until recently, the knowledge about
the relationship between ORP level and BES addition was still lim-
ited. For VFA production, reactor AN + BES accelerated acid yields
after day 5, and maximal VFA concentration (23.09 g/L) was
obtained on day 11 (Fig. 2a). The VFA production in AN + BES reac-
tors was higher than that in AN, which correlated with its ORP level
between 100 and 200 mV before day 6. ORP decreased and VFA
accumulated slowed after day 6. The other possible reason for
higher VFA production in AN + BES reactors was that methanegen-
esis was inhibited by BES to promote the VFA accumulation. How-
ever, there was little methane production (less than 5%) in 21-day
fermentation (data not shown). In addition, BES addition had no
effect on VFA composition (Fig. 2b).
From the above results, we concluded that less negative ORP
levels (100 to 200 mV) would play a positive role in VFA pro-
duction. Under limited aeration conditions, inoculating anaerobic
sludge would beneﬁt higher VFA yield from more facultative acido-
gens. In addition, BES addition indeed improved VFA accumulation
in acidogenic fermentation. Reasons for all these phenomena were
analyzed as follows.
3.2. Hydrolysis of organic matters for VFA production from FW
3.2.1. Carbohydrates solubilization
VFA production is closely related to hydrolysis and degrada-
tion of substrates. Soluble sugar reﬂects a balance between rates
of solubilization and degradation (Fig. 3a). On day 1, concentra-
tions of soluble sugar decreased in LA + AnS, AN, AN + BES reac-
tors,

tors, degradation of carbohydrates played the dominant role from
the beginning of fermentation. After day 1, soluble sugar concen-
trations decreased rapidly in all reactors. However, the uptake
rates of soluble sugar were different in each reactor as follows:

3.2.2. Proteins solubilization and ammonia nitrogen release
During the whole fermentation process, there were downward
trends for soluble proteins under all conditions (Fig. 3b). LA + AnS
reactors had the most soluble proteins. Soluble protein concentra-
tions in AN reactors remained relatively stable during the fermen-
tation and just decreased from 2000 to 1200 mg/L. These results
demonstrated that less negative ORP levels (100 to 200 mV)
could promote proteins solubilization. It was likely that limited
aeration environment could stimulate the effective co-existence
of facultative bacteria and anaerobes (Sang et al., 2009) and low
oxygen promoted fermentative bacteria to excrete enzymes (Lim
et al., 2014). After day 15, the concentration levels of soluble pro-
teins almost kept unchanged under all conditions, which indicated
there was a balance between dissolution and degradation of pro-
tein. Interestingly, at the end of fermentation, some soluble pro-
teins were still undegraded in all reactors.
The proteins in FW are ﬁrst degraded to amino acids, then to
ammonia, VFAs and other products. Consequently, ammonia
(NH4
+-N) is generally used to assess the level of protein degrada-
tion. For all conditions, NH4
+-N concentrations remained low and
stable before day 9 (Fig. 3c). After day 9, NH4
+-N concentration

Based on the above results, we assured that less negative ORP
levels (100 to 200 mV) had a positive effect on substrates
degradation, especially proteins. And inoculating anaerobic sludge
would beneﬁt substrates transformation. The higher organics
degradation efﬁciency led to more VFA accumulation.
3.3. The activities of key enzymes
Carbohydrates ﬁrstly hydrolyze into monosacchride, mean-
while proteins hydrolyze into amino acids, and then they all turn
into pyruvate. So we next measured activities of a-glucosidase
and protease under four conditions during the acidogenic fermen-
tation. As shown in Fig. 4a, there were the same trends of a-
glucosidase activities for all reactors before day 9. With the
decrease of carbohydrates in FW, a-glucosidase activities for all
reactors decreased to about 4.0 U/g VS on day 9. It was likely that
carbohydrates were hydrolyzed completely, reducing enzyme
activities. But afterwards, a-glucosidase activities increased in AN
and AN + BES reactors. On the contrary, they continued to decline
in LA + AnS and LA + AeS reactors. Since soluble sugars were almost
completely degraded quickly before day 9, the impact of a-
glucosidase activity increased was unclear.
Apparently, during the whole fermentation, protease activities
in LA + AnS reactors were higher than those in other reactors,
which explained the phenomenon described above that soluble
protein concentration was higher and degradation rate was faster
under LA + AnS conditions. The improved hydrolysis could be
attributed to the stimulation of fermentative bacteria to excrete
hydrolytic enzymes under micro-aeration condition (Xu et al.,
2014a). After day 15, the protease activities for all reactors were
as follows: FWLA+AnS > FWAN > FWAN+BES > FWLA+AeS. Overall, pro-
tease activity in LA + AeS reactors was the lowest throughout the
fermentation. It was supposed that hydrolysis of proteins was
the rate-limiting step in acidogenic fermentation (Wang et al.,
2016), and aerobic sludge was not suitable to be used as an inocu-
lum for acidogenesis from FW.
3.4. The microbial structure analysis
We speculated that the differences in VFA productions and
enzyme activities of these reactors were related to the structure
of microbial community. 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing
was performed to determine the contribution of the microbial
community to the reactor outcome. We identiﬁed 32 phyla in LA
+ AnS reactors, 28 in AN + BES, 25 in LA + AeS, and 22 in AN. The
majority of sequences belonged to phyla Firmicutes, Proteobacteria,
and Bacteroidetes for all reactors at the time of maximum VFA pro-
duction (Fig. 5a). The sum of these three phyla accounted for 71.3%
(LA + AnS), 83.4% (AN + BES), 84.3% (LA + AeS) and 93.5% (AN) of
the total reads. This result showed the higher microbial diversity
under LA + AnS conditions. Phylum Firmicutes was the highest
under limited aeration conditions (42.2% for LA + AnS, 48.2% for
LA + AeS) and the lowest in AN reactors (21.1%). However, com-
pared to LA + AnS (11.0%) and LA + AeS (0.3%), phylum Bacteroide-

Phylum Firmicutes is facultative bacteria, which is known to pro-
duce cellulases, lipases, proteases and other extracellular enzymes
(Leven et al., 2007). Bacteroidetes have been reported that they can
exist in obligate fermentation and acidiﬁcation bioreactors (Lim
et al., 2014). Interestingly, phylum Chloroﬂexi was absent under
anaerobic conditions. Most of Chloroﬂexi are ﬁlamentous bacteria,
and they have the ability to degrade macromolecular organics
(Yu et al., 2016).
At a class level, most of the reads (119 classes identiﬁed in total)
belonged to 13 classes (Fig. 5b), mainly with four classes (Clostridia,
Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria and Bacteroidia). Clostri-
dia (about 40%) within Firmicutes was the dominant class under
limited aeration conditions, but under anaerobic conditions there
were a great number of Bacteroidia within Bacteroidetes (more than
35%).
Genus level characterization showed that the initial samples of
three systems (LA + AnS, AN, AN + BES) were clustered together,
indicating the microbial community structure were similar in
these reactors at the start of fermentation because of the same
inoculum AnS (Fig. 6). During the acidogenesis, a remarkable
increase in microbial diversity was observed in LA + AnS reactor.
Larger amounts of Anaeroﬁlum (30.8%), Clostridium (4.1%), Pseu-
domonas (3.9%), Prevotella (5.8%), Oscillospira (2.6%), Ruminococcus
(2.3%), Brevundimonas (1.7%) were detected under this condition.
Clostridium, Oscillospira, Anaeroﬁlum and Ruminococcus within Fir-
micutes have been shown to dominate FW acidogenic reactors
(Grootscholten et al., 2013; Mgrootscholten et al., 2014). The

dominance of Firmicutes indicates the ability of acidogenic reactor
to metabolize various substrates, such as proteins, carbohydrates,
and lipids (Lim et al., 2014). Pseudomonas, Prevotella and Brevundi-
monas previously demonstrate high ability of acidogenesis. There-
fore, more soluble substrates and VFA production in LA + AnS
reactors were correlated with the predominance of Firmicutes
and some other acidogens. Paradoxically, although Clostridium also
accounted for higher proportion (45.0%) in LA + AeS reactors, the
VFA yield was the least on account of the less microbial diversity
and less Clostridium in absolute amount in aerobic sludge for FW
acidogenesis.
By contrast, the abundance of Bacteroides apparently increased
in AN (63.6%) and AN + BES (40.9%) reactors, a reﬂection of the
anaerobic environment. Nevertheless, presumably because of the
presence of BES, a clear distinction of microbial community diver-
sity was present in these two anaerobic reactors. Some studies ﬁnd
that long-term exposure to BES not only eliminate Archaea but also
alter the bacterial community structure by acting as a competing
electron acceptor for some microorganisms (Chiu and Lee, 2001;
Ye et al., 1999). Signiﬁcantly, the abundance of Methanogenus
was less than 1% under both AN and AN + BES conditions. There
were some other dominant genera such as Proteus (15.0%), Provi-
dencia (17.2%), Prevotella (1.4%) in AN + BES reactors, which were
hardly detected in AN. Higher VFA production in AN + BES mainly
was attributed to the wide existence of Proteus and Providencia that
could degrade organics to acids. These results implied that the low
VFA production under anaerobic conditions was not caused by
methanogenesis.
4. Conclusions
The optimal ORP level for VFA production was 100 to
200 mV, which could be obtained by limited aeration during aci-
dogenic fermentation. At this ORP level, anaerobic sludge as an
inoculum promoted the degradation of substrates, especially pro-
tein, and thus enhanced VFA yield. Anaerobic condition (ORP
200 to 300 mV) was not suitable for VFA production at pH
6.0. Higher VFA yield appeared to depend on the greater abun-
dance of Firmicutes and more diverse microbial community under
LA + AnS conditions. BES addition in acidogenesis would improve
VFA yield by increasing abundance of some acidogens rather than
its inhibition to methanogenesis.
